---
title: "Implementing the passage-level Student-t model in Stan"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

We have now assembled the main pieces of a posterior sampler. HMC uses the log
posterior and its gradient to construct a trajectory. A mass matrix adjusts
that trajectory to the posterior's global scale and orientation. NUTS chooses
how far the trajectory grows. Writing all of those pieces by hand for every
model would be possible, but it would also make it easy to introduce a
mistake in a derivative, transformation, or transition.

[Stan](https://mc-stan.org/) asks us to describe the statistical model and
handles those sampling calculations. More specifically, we declare (i) the
observed values and fixed constants, (ii) the unknown parameters and their
constraints, and (iii) the log-density contributions supplied by the prior
and likelihood. Stan differentiates the resulting log density and uses NUTS
to generate dependent draws from the posterior.

Okay. So how do we translate the passage-level Student-$t$ model into those
declarations?

We will read the program from top to bottom. For each block, we will first ask
what mathematical object it represents and then ask what Stan does with that
object. This order matters because code that runs successfully may still
encode a different model from the one we intended.

## The complete program

The mathematical model from the
[robust location--scale discussion](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#a-robust-location-scale-model)
is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_j\mid\mu,\sigma
&\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}t_4(\mu,\sigma),
&&j=1,\ldots,55,\\ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
\mu&\sim\mathcal N(0,s_\mu^2),\\
\sigma&\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,s_\sigma^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

The first line says that once $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are fixed, the 55 passage
summaries are [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) draws from the
same Student-$t$ distribution. The next two lines state the prior
distributions. The value $\nu=4$ is treated as a fixed constant in this model,
so it belongs with the data rather than with the unknown parameters.

```stan
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  vector[N] y;
  real<lower=0> prior_mu_sd;
  real<lower=0> prior_sigma_sd;
  real<lower=2> nu;
}

parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

model {
  mu ~ normal(0, prior_mu_sd);
  sigma ~ normal(0, prior_sigma_sd);
  y ~ student_t(nu, mu, sigma);
}

generated quantities {
  real geometric_duration_ratio = exp(mu);
  array[N] real y_rep;
  vector[N] log_lik;

  for (n in 1:N) {
    y_rep[n] = student_t_rng(nu, mu, sigma);
    log_lik[n] = student_t_lpdf(y[n] | nu, mu, sigma);
  }
}
```

The `data` block contains quantities known before sampling begins. `N` records
the number of modeled rows; `y` contains the observed contrast in each row;
the two prior scales set $s_\mu$ and $s_\sigma$; and `nu` sets the fixed degrees
of freedom. Writing `vector[N] y` tells Stan both that `y` is a real-valued
vector and that its length must match `N`.

The `parameters` block contains quantities whose posterior distribution we
want to compute. `mu` can take any real value. The declaration
`real<lower=0> sigma` restricts `sigma` to positive values because a negative
scale has no meaning in the Student-$t$ density.

The `model` block adds the log-density terms that define the posterior kernel.
The statement

```stan
y ~ student_t(nu, mu, sigma);
```

is a compact way to add

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{N}\log t_\nu(y_j\mid\mu,\sigma)
$$

to Stan's internal log density, which Stan calls `target`. The statement does
not generate new values of `y`. The two prior statements add the log prior
density of `mu` and `sigma` in the same way.

The positivity constraint and the prior perform different jobs. The constraint
sets the possible values of `sigma`. The zero-centered normal density assigns
relative prior density across those positive values. Because the omitted
normalizing factor of two is constant in `sigma`, the constrained normal
density has the half-normal shape required by the posterior kernel.

Stan carries out HMC in an unconstrained space. For a positive parameter, it
uses an internal real-valued coordinate $\lambda$ and maps it to the reported
parameter by $\sigma=\exp(\lambda)$. This transformation changes interval
widths. For instance, the interval from $\lambda=0$ to $\lambda=.1$ maps to <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->
approximately $\sigma=1$ through $1.105$, a width of about $.105$. The
equal-width interval from $\lambda=2$ to $\lambda=2.1$ maps to approximately <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->
$7.389$ through $8.166$, a width of about $.777$. Equal intervals on the
$\lambda$ scale therefore represent unequal intervals on the $\sigma$ scale.

The [Jacobian discussion](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#jacobians-as-local-stretching)
named the derivative that records this local stretching. In one dimension,
the Jacobian is simply the absolute derivative of the transformation. Here

$$
\left|\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right|
=\exp(\lambda)=\sigma.
$$

Multiplying the density by this local stretch preserves probability when we
change coordinates; on the log scale, multiplication becomes addition, so
the adjustment is $\log\sigma$. Stan adds this adjustment automatically for
the declared constraint. Adding it again in the `model` block would count the
same transformation twice.

| Mathematical object | Stan statement | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,s_\mu)$ | `mu ~ normal(0, prior_mu_sd)` | add the location-prior log density |
| $\sigma\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,s_\sigma)$ | lower bound plus `sigma ~ normal(...)` | restrict support and add the half-normal shape |
| $Y_j\mid\mu,\sigma\sim t_\nu(\mu,\sigma)$ | `y ~ student_t(nu, mu, sigma)` | add all 55 conditionally independent likelihood terms |
| $\exp(\mu)$ | `geometric_duration_ratio = exp(mu)` | transform each joint posterior draw |
| $\widetilde Y_j$ | `student_t_rng(...)` | simulate one replicated passage contrast |
| $\log p(y_j\mid\mu,\sigma)$ | `student_t_lpdf(...)` | retain one pointwise log-likelihood contribution |

## Preparing the observed data

```{r}
#| label: prepare-provo-stan-data
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
stan_data <- list(
  N = length(y),
  y = y,
  prior_mu_sd = 2 * sd(y),
  prior_sigma_sd = 2 * sd(y),
  nu = 4
)

stopifnot(stan_data$N == 55L, all(is.finite(stan_data$y)))
str(stan_data)
```

## Fitting the exact model

The reference run uses four data-scaled initial values constructed from the posterior grid covariance shown on the [mass-matrix page](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd). Recall that [covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) is the expected product of centered quantities and records joint scale and orientation. The code below reconstructs those values from the observed Provo contrasts rather than relying on an undeclared helper.

```{r}
#| label: construct-provo-stan-initial-values
#| code-fold: true
log_posterior_pair <- function(parameter_pair) {
  mu <- parameter_pair[[1L]]
  sigma <- exp(parameter_pair[[2L]])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = stan_data$nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, stan_data$prior_mu_sd, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, stan_data$prior_sigma_sd, log = TRUE) +
    parameter_pair[[2L]]
}

gradient_log_posterior_pair <- function(parameter_pair) {
  mu <- parameter_pair[[1L]]
  sigma <- exp(parameter_pair[[2L]])
  residual <- y - mu
  scaled_squared <- residual^2 / sigma^2
  c(
    sum((stan_data$nu + 1) * residual /
          (stan_data$nu * sigma^2 + residual^2)) -
      mu / stan_data$prior_mu_sd^2,
    sum(-1 + (stan_data$nu + 1) * scaled_squared /
          (stan_data$nu + scaled_squared)) -
      sigma^2 / stan_data$prior_sigma_sd^2 + 1
  )
}

mode_fit <- optim(
  c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
  function(parameter_pair) -log_posterior_pair(parameter_pair),
  gr = function(parameter_pair) -gradient_log_posterior_pair(parameter_pair),
  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L)
)
mode_pair <- unname(mode_fit$par)
mode_covariance <- solve(mode_fit$hessian)
grid_sd <- sqrt(diag(mode_covariance))
posterior_grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(mode_pair[[1L]] - 7 * grid_sd[[1L]],
           mode_pair[[1L]] + 7 * grid_sd[[1L]], length.out = 321L),
  log_sigma = seq(mode_pair[[2L]] - 7 * grid_sd[[2L]],
                  mode_pair[[2L]] + 7 * grid_sd[[2L]], length.out = 321L)
)
posterior_grid$log_kernel <- apply(posterior_grid, 1L, log_posterior_pair)
posterior_grid$weight <- exp(
  posterior_grid$log_kernel - max(posterior_grid$log_kernel)
)
posterior_grid$weight <- posterior_grid$weight / sum(posterior_grid$weight)
grid_mean_pair <- colSums(posterior_grid * posterior_grid$weight)
grid_centered <- sweep(as.matrix(posterior_grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")]),
                       2L, grid_mean_pair, "-")
grid_covariance <- crossprod(grid_centered * sqrt(posterior_grid$weight))

initial_values <- function(offsets) {
  lapply(offsets, function(offset) list(
    mu = mode_pair[[1L]] + offset * sqrt(grid_covariance[1L, 1L]),
    sigma = exp(mode_pair[[2L]] +
                  offset * sqrt(grid_covariance[2L, 2L]))
  ))
}

stopifnot(mode_fit$convergence == 0L)
stan_offsets <- seq(-.75, .75, length.out = 4L)
do.call(rbind, initial_values(stan_offsets))
```

The sampling call is then fully specified by the observed data, the program, and these initial values.

Four chains provide independent starting trajectories for between-chain
comparison. The 750 warmup iterations adapt step size and mass geometry; the
1,000 retained iterations per chain determine the available Monte Carlo
information. `adapt_delta = .90` favors relatively accurate integration,
while `max_treedepth = 10` bounds work per transition. How can we tell whether
these settings worked well enough for this posterior? The following pages use
the retained chains to ask whether they reached the same region, moved through
it efficiently, and followed its geometry accurately.

```{r}
#| label: show-provo-stan-fit
#| eval: false
library(cmdstanr)

model <- cmdstan_model(
  "scripts/data-grounding/reference_inference_bayesian.stan",
  quiet = TRUE
)

fit <- model$sample(
  data = stan_data,
  seed = 2026101806,
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = 4,
  iter_warmup = 750,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  adapt_delta = .90,
  max_treedepth = 10,
  init = initial_values(stan_offsets),
  refresh = 0,
  output_dir = tempdir()
)
```

The summaries below use the 4,000 retained draws from these four chains. We
will summarize $\mu$, $\sigma$, and $\exp(\mu)$, while retaining chain identity
for the convergence checks on the following pages.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-provo-stan-fit
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)
production <- subset_draws(
  cache$production_draws,
  variable = c("mu", "sigma", "geometric_duration_ratio")
)
fit_summary <- as.data.frame(summarise_draws(
  production,
  "mean", "median", "sd", "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail",
  ~quantile2(.x, probs = c(.025, .975))
))
production_diagnostics <- as.data.frame(
  as_draws_df(cache$production_diagnostics)
)

stopifnot(max(fit_summary$rhat) < 1.01,
          sum(production_diagnostics$divergent__) == 0L)
fit_summary
```

The fitted mean of $\mu$ is `r sprintf("%.6f", fit_summary$mean[fit_summary$variable == "mu"])`, and the geometric-scale ratio has mean `r sprintf("%.6f", fit_summary$mean[fit_summary$variable == "geometric_duration_ratio"])`. Because the model receives one aggregated contrast per passage, these summaries describe the passage-level Student-t distribution. Estimating participant-level duration effects would require the raw reader observations and a model containing participant variation.

## Factorization and adequacy

The vectorized likelihood represents

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{55}\log t_4(y_j\mid\mu,\sigma).
$$

Concise code does not make passages a probability sample or recover reader-level measurements. Stan can correctly sample the declared posterior even when the declared model is scientifically inadequate. Computation, prior implications, posterior prediction, and the correspondence between rows and modeled units require separate checks.

## Recap and forward link

1. The data block contains observed values and fixed constants; the parameters block declares unknowns.
2. Constraints define support and transformations, while priors define density on that support.
3. Each model statement corresponds to a prior or likelihood term in the posterior factorization.
4. Successful sampling validates neither aggregation nor the observation model.

The [trace-plot page](checking-markov-chains.qmd#production-traces) begins the diagnostic sequence using these fitted draws.

## Check your understanding

1. Which objects belong in the data block?
2. How do the positivity constraint and half-normal prior differ?
3. What do tilde statements add to `target`?
4. Why does successful sampling not validate the aggregation scheme?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Observed quantities and fixed constants belong in `data`: here $N$, `y`, the two prior scales, and $\nu$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The lower bound defines the parameter's support and transformation; the zero-centered normal density supplies the half-normal prior shape on that support. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Each tilde statement adds the corresponding log-density or log-mass contribution, up to constants, to `target`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Stan can sample the declared passage-level posterior correctly even if aggregation discarded readers or the likelihood poorly represents the scientific design. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
